record.paper_title: Braking index of isolated pulsars: open questions and ways forward
record.original_question: Can the pulsar braking law be modeled as the polynomial spin-down equation Ω̇ = −s(t)Ω − r(t)Ω³ − g(t)Ω⁵, where s(t), r(t), and g(t) represent wind, magnetic-dipole-radiation, and quadrupole torque mechanisms respectively, so that known low-frequency braking-index measurements can be fitted without detailed knowledge of magnetic-field or composition evolution, the combined wind and magnetic-dipole terms can constrain the magnetic field, and high-frequency extensions can probe mechanisms involving mass, composition, magnetic field, or other neutron-star properties?

evidence.quote: Another approach to this problem considered by Alvarez et. al. [21] is to ex- pand the braking law itself into a polynomial which consists of all assum ed torque mechanisms. In this way, we can assume there are no changes in the magnetic ﬁeld, composition of the star, magnetosphere, etc., and that the pulsa r is rotating at low frequency.

As shown in [21] the braking law can be expanded as, ˙Ω = −s(t)Ω − r(t)Ω3 − g(t)Ω5, (7) where s(t), r(t), and g(t) are functions representing the wind, MDR, and quadrupole torque mechanisms respectively, and Ω is the rotational frequenc y.

Furthermore, the combination of s(t) and r(t) may constrain the magnetic ﬁeld. The polynomial solution may also be expanded into high f requencies which may give insight into other mechanisms at work such as mass, co mposition, magnetic ﬁeld, etc.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let Ω(t) > 0 denote the rotational angular frequency of an isolated rotating neutron star, and consider the polynomial spin-down model

    Ω̇(t) = −s(t) Ω(t) − r(t) Ω(t)^3 − g(t) Ω(t)^5,

where s(t), r(t), g(t) are nonnegative time-dependent coefficients representing, respectively, a particle-wind torque, a magnetic-dipole-radiation torque, and a (mass) quadrupole gravitational-radiation torque. For such a model define the (instantaneous) braking index by

    n(t) := Ω(t) Ω̈(t) / Ω̇(t)^2.

Address the following questions:

(a) Show that, for slowly rotating pulsars (Ω small enough that the Ω^5 term is negligible) and under the assumption that s, r are slowly varying compared with Ω, the model can be made consistent with any observed braking index n ∈ ℝ by an appropriate choice of the pair (s(t), r(t)), and characterize the family of such pairs (s,r) that fit a given finite set of measurements {(Ω_i, Ω̇_i, Ω̈_i)}.

(b) Determine to what extent the combination of s(t) and r(t) extracted in (a) constrains the surface magnetic-field strength B, given the standard magnetic-dipole relation r(t) ∝ B(t)^2 (with explicit proportionality constants depending on stellar moment of inertia and geometry), without assuming any prior evolution law for B or for the stellar composition.

(c) For rapidly rotating pulsars, where the Ω^5 term is non-negligible, decide whether the three coefficients (s(t), r(t), g(t)) can be uniquely identified from rotational observables (Ω, Ω̇, Ω̈, and higher derivatives), and identify what additional physical inputs (e.g. relating g(t) to the mass-quadrupole ellipticity) are needed for unique reconstruction.

The problem is to establish whether this polynomial ansatz provides a fitting framework for known low-frequency braking-index measurements without invoking detailed magnetic-field or composition evolution, and to determine its predictive power at high frequencies.
artifact.status_search_result: The polynomial three-term spin-down ansatz Ω̇ = −sΩ − rΩ^3 − gΩ^5 is a standard phenomenological model in pulsar timing (Alvarez & Carramiñana style), but no general identifiability/fitting theorem is established. Subsequent literature (e.g. analyses of braking indices for Crab-like and high-n pulsars) treats it as an underdetermined modeling proposal rather than a settled mathematical result; the underlying physical question of which torque mix governs real pulsars remains open.

status_evidence.title: Braking index of isolated pulsars
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews open questions about pulsar braking indices and notes the polynomial torque expansion as one approach still under investigation.
status_evidence.claim: The polynomial torque-expansion approach is presented as an open modeling avenue rather than a resolved problem.
